tracks.title: Where did the history go
tracks.text: Lesson 01 point 5 — git. This one is a deep dive, under the workbook lesson… so it leans on that page's anatomy. Where did the history go. [curious] Here's the worry. Your project's history is already scattered, and you stopped noticing. First… code lives in git. Second… content lives in a CMS. Third… your application data lives in some SaaS. And fourth… the record of what got deployed when lives in a dashboard's audit log — a list you can read, but never clone. Four histories… four homes… none of them the same shape. Now make the whole app one HTML file. The worry sharpens. A single-file artifact smells like a binary. Did you just lose version control entirely? Where do the diffs live? Is your history locked inside someone's platform? [excited] That's the right fear. And the answer is better than don't worry about it. Nothing about this format ever stopped being text… and the project running it was a repo the whole time.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Here, git isn't a tool you bolt on — it's a property of the project. The source rides inside the artifact as plain text. And the running project's data root is a real git repo… so history, diff, and rollback come for free. The engine says this in its own words — a git-backed store, the versioned source of truth, making the per-tenant data root a git repo to buy history, diff, and rollback for free. Not integrates with git. It is a git repo. One per tenant… git-initialized the moment the project starts living.

tracks.title: What actually diffs
tracks.text: What actually diffs. Here's the line the whole lesson hangs on. Git the source… ship the artifact… and the artifact carries the source back out. A workbook is three forms at once, and they diff differently. Picture three rows. First row… the org spec — plain text, in a script block. Its verdict: clean line diffs. This is the designed diff surface. Second row… the HTML artifact — text, end to end. Diffable in principle, because it's text, not a blob — and when you want the legible version, you read the org source underneath. Third row… the SQLite disk — a binary database file. The verdict there is honest: git stores it, but it can't line-diff it. And the move when it doesn't is to unbundle it back into a source tree. So two things follow. First… the source is never trapped — a workbook ships as a bundle, a plain zip carrying the HTML and the org side by side, on purpose… so a recipient can unbundle and re-author. Second… the one binary layer, SQLite, is the one place to be careful — and we come back to it honestly, rather than pretend it diffs.

tracks.title: Every deploy is a commit
tracks.text: Every deploy is a commit. [excited] This is the load-bearing fact. When you deploy, the runtime does two things in one breath. It writes the fast SQLite index your app reads from… and it commits your org source into the tenant repo. One deploy… one commit… with a real message and a real author. Picture the flow as a sequence. You hand the CLI a name and an org file — deploy lander. The runtime fans it into two stores. To one side, it writes the fast index it serves from. To the other, it calls save and commits, with the message deploy lander. Git hands back a short hash — nine f three c two a b. And that hash comes back to you as the receipt. Now the history comes straight back out, with commands you already know. Log gives you a list — nine f three c two a b, deploy lander… four d one e zero c seven, deploy report… and so on. And diff is literally git diff HEAD-til-one HEAD — the last deploy, as a unified diff. So what did that deploy change… stops being a dashboard question with a vendor-shaped answer. It's a git diff. The same answer you'd get for any repo on your machine.

tracks.title: Who is the author
tracks.text: Who is the author. This is a depth rung — skippable if you just want the shape. A commit needs an author. And here, the author isn't a config field you forgot to set — it's who you are. The engine bridges auth's WHO straight into git's attribution. The author name defaults to the tenant. The email is tenant-at-workbooks-dot-local. And every commit sets the git author and committer from that one identity. In the module's own words — git's attribution is auth's WHO. Underneath the name sits real cryptographic identity. Each tenant gets an Ed25519 keypair, kept private and never committed. From its public key, the engine derives a did-key — a genuine W3C decentralized identifier, the same shape Radicle uses. Picture the flow. Auth identity flows two ways. Down one path… into the git author and committer environment. Down the other… into the Ed25519 key, and on to the did-key. Both arrive at the commit — authored, attributable. And one more arrow leaves the commit, into the run ledger. Because an agent run leaves a hash-chained ledger — a sha-256 fold over its steps from a genesis hash — and its head gets committed to git… so the head is witnessed by git's own content-addressing. The chain proves the steps. Git proves when the chain's head existed. Two independent witnesses… one repo.

tracks.title: The agent's git hand
tracks.text: The agent's git hand. Agents commit too — but they don't get a shell. The hand is host-brokered. The agent supplies only a commit message, and the host decides every word of the command line. There's no native-bash hatch here; the one that used to exist was deleted on purpose. The agent says what… the engine does how. Walk the sequence. The agent calls commit-and-push with one message — add tuesday post. Then the host takes over, in order. First… it writes the gitignore from the private boundary. Second… git add dash A. Third… commit, with hooks off and the author email set. Fourth… push to origin, if a remote exists. And fifth… publish — mirroring the content and blog folders live. Then a string comes back. And those shapes are exact. You get nine f three c two a b, pushed, when a remote took it. Or, committed, no origin remote to push, when there's nowhere to go yet. Or a trailing push-failed note, capped at a hundred and twenty characters, when the remote refuses. Honest receipts… not silent success. And that last step earns its place — commit implies publish, atomically. After the commit lands, publish mirrors the content and blog folders to the live site… so committed always implies live. This wasn't a flourish — it was a fix. [sighs] A lander once shipped blog posts that were committed to the repo… but served 404… because the run died before a separate publish step ever ran. Now there is no separate step to die before. Commit… and it's live.

tracks.title: The gitignore nobody writes
tracks.text: The gitignore nobody writes. A brokered add dash A is a sharp tool — a bulk add can sweep in anything in the tree, including a signing key. So the danger is defused before it can happen. Every tenant repo gets a gitignore written from one boundary module — Private — and that same module is consulted by git, by the bundler, and by the library… so the line can't drift. One definition of private… three enforcers. Here's what it keeps out, and why. First… the workbooks folder — that's the Ed25519 signing key, the one that must never leave. Second… the memory folder — an agent's working memory, the session, not the work. Third… the beads and claude folders — task data and assistant scratch, born from a real leak. Fourth… scratch and tmp — transient space, nobody's history. And last… the underscore sidecars — the steps log, the status file, the trace, the telemetry database, the ledger. The doctrine behind that list is one sentence, and it's worth keeping. Sharing exposes work… never the session that produced it. It's a scarred rule — it exists because beads task data once got pushed to GitHub, and the boundary module is the repair. [excited] And here's the elegant part. The library reuses git's own matcher — check-ignore — to decide what ships when you share. So the agent's native git instinct… is the don't-share marker. The thing that keeps bytes out of a push is the same thing that keeps bytes out of a share. You only have to be right once.

tracks.title: A second ledger, jj
tracks.text: A second ledger — jj. Another depth rung… skip it freely. On top of the same repo sits an optional second record. The JJ module colocates Jujutsu directly onto the git repo. Same commits… plus an operation log. Every change to the repo state is itself a recorded, addressable, undoable operation. Git records the commits. JJ records the moves between them. Picture it as one repo splitting into two rails. Down one rail… git commits, content-addressed history. Down the other… the jj op-log, replayable state changes. And both rails arrive at the same place — tamper-evident, from two directions. Two reasons it's there. First… it corroborates the signed ledger from a moment ago — the run history becomes tamper-evident from two independent directions at once. Second… it's the substrate for concurrent sub-agents — jj auto-rebases the text, while org validations arbitrate the meaning. And it's a no-op if jj isn't installed… so it costs nothing where it isn't wanted.

tracks.title: The repo you already have
tracks.text: The repo you already have. Here's the antidote to locked in your platform. One verb pushes your whole history to your forge. It's plain git push underneath… so it works with GitHub, GitLab, Gitea, or anything self-hosted. The forge tools only exist to provision a remote the first time. Picture the tenant repo with three roads out. First road… an explicit URL — that's a bare git push, no forge tool needed at all. Second road… a forge name, like github — and the gh tool provisions the remote and pushes. Third road… radicle, for peer-to-peer, addressed by DID. The common case is one line — mirror github. With no origin yet, it runs gh repo create, names it wb-dev, makes it private, and pushes. Back comes okay, plus the URL. If you already have the remote, skip the forge tool entirely — hand mirror a URL and it's a bare push, zero tooling. And when nothing's installed, the engine doesn't fail quietly — it tells you the truth… no forge CLI on PATH, create the remote yourself and use mirror. For the peer-to-peer crowd, federate runs rad init and hands back a Radicle ID… with delegates addressed by the same DID from earlier, doing real work.

tracks.title: History as a public surface
tracks.text: History as a public surface. Because the project is a repo… its changelog can be its actual log — not a marketing timeline somebody curated. A deployed app serves a changes endpoint on its public plane. Anonymous… read-only… the real git log, newest-first, capped at thirty entries, paired with the keeper's status. Picture the shape it returns. A changes list… each entry a short hash, a timestamp, an author, and a message — nine f three c two a b, deploy lander… then four d one e zero c seven, deploy report. Plus an agent field carrying the keeper status. The authed sibling carries the same idea, and its comment states the point — the changelog is verifiable history, not marketing. Anyone can read it. Anyone can clone the repo and check it. The page narrates its own construction… from facts it can't fake. That's the outbound direction. The inbound direction — a push to your forge reconciling back into the live project — is real, but it lives next door. Pull snapshots a dirty tree first, aborts cleanly on conflict rather than clobbering agent data, and rides a keeper trigger. That whole reconcile loop is its own lesson — gitops. This page owns the artifact-and-history side.

tracks.title: Where this is honest
tracks.text: Where this is honest. None of the hard edges are hidden — they're in the code's own comments. So here they are plainly. First… SQLite is binary. Git stores the disk file, but can't line-diff it. The plan is a legible projection — readable SQL dumps GitHub could render — but that's design direction, not shipped behavior. There's no dump emitter today. Second… Radicle needs peers. A clone wants at least two nodes online, and rad's keys are per-device with no external-key import — an upstream limitation, not missing code on our side. Third… inbound app builds still ride CI. The reconcile loop integrates upstream changes, but rebuilding the app from them leans on a CI bridge for now. Fourth… auto-provision needs a forge tool. No gh, glab, or tea on PATH means you create the remote yourself — the plain-push rail always works regardless. And last… running git in a container is real ops. [sighs] Every git op passes a safe-directory flag for a reason. On deployed boxes, the data volume's user-id differs from the runtime's… and git's dubious-ownership guard refuses every command — silently blocking commit and publish. That bit a set of agents who wrote stories to disk for days… that never shipped. The flag is the scar.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can I just git-init my workbook source directory? Yes — that's the native mode, not a workaround. The source is org text; nothing about the format fights git. The running project just does it for you, one repo per tenant. Is my history locked inside the runtime? No. It's plain git. Mirror pushes the whole history to your forge with a bare push — no platform tool required when you bring the URL. What diffs badly? The SQLite disk — it's a binary database. Your source, and the unpacked tree, are the legible diff surface. Do agent commits pollute my history? No — they're authored, each with a real author and a message, and code paths stay separate from data paths. [chuckles] And does this replace GitHub? No — it pushes to it. The runtime hosts a repo; GitHub stays your forge.

tracks.title: Back up to the workbook
tracks.text: So that's git, here. Not a tool you bolt on… a property of the project. The source rides inside the artifact, the running project is a real repo, every deploy is a commit you can clone and diff… and your history mirrors to the forge you already have. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This deep dive stands on its parent — the workbook — lesson one. Read that for the anatomy this page assumed… and if you want the inbound half, the push-to-update loop, that's gitops, waiting next door.
